name: Heightpill / short-king discourse

lead: The heightpill is a forum belief that a man's height heavily determines his dating and social success. It is why many people in looksmaxxing and dating forums get interested in lifts, posture and height-gain methods to look taller. 'Short king' discourse pushes back, celebrating shorter men.

Research on heightism, a term coined by Saul Feldman in 1971, has reported links between height and earnings, partner preferences and some mental health measures, with cross-cultural differences suggesting preferences are partly shaped by culture. The size and cause of those links are debated.

paras: It is a belief framework rather than a practice. It is discussed alongside height-related measures such as footwear, posture and, more rarely, surgery.

No direct risks from the discourse are documented in published sources, though researchers have noted that dissatisfaction with height can affect attention and mood. Height-increasing surgery carries its own medical risks.

angle.text: Looksmaxxing and dating forums use the heightpill to argue height strongly shapes romantic outcomes, which drives interest in lifts, posture and height-gain methods for a taller-looking presentation, while short-king discourse pushes back. Research finds height correlations with dating outcomes; their size and cause are debated.

lead: The heightpill is a term in looksmaxxing and related online communities for the belief that a man's height is among the most decisive factors in his romantic and social outcomes, and that it is largely fixed. 'Short king' discourse is the counter-current: a mainstream, often humorous movement that celebrates shorter men and disputes the idea that height determines their prospects. For appearance, the discourse matters because it shapes which height-related options people explore: shoe lifts, posture and fitness work to look taller, grooming and style for those who accept their height, and in some cases surgical limb lengthening.[1][2]

Prejudice based on height has been studied under the name heightism, a term credited to sociologist Saul Feldman in 1971.[3] Published research has reported associations between height and earnings, partner preferences and some mental health measures. Studies of real couples show that height preferences are reflected in pairings but modestly, and cross-cultural work suggests preferences are partly shaped by culture.[3][4][5]
This article documents how the idea is framed, how the two camps talk about it, and what research on height has reported. It does not take a position on how much height matters for any individual.

paras: In the vocabulary of the manosphere and looksmaxxing forums, a 'pill' is a worldview-changing realisation, borrowed from the red pill and blue pill imagery of the 1999 film The Matrix. The heightpill is the view that height acts as a gatekeeping trait, particularly for men's dating success, and that it cannot be offset easily by other traits. Wikipedia describes the black pill ideology associated with looksmaxxing as holding that female sexual selection rests mainly on external traits such as height and facial attractiveness.[1] On the forums the heightpill is usually listed next to other 'pills' such as the racepill and the facepill, and members compare which is most decisive.[6][7]

Looksmaxxing itself is described as an online practice focused on maximising men's physical attractiveness, with methods ranging from skincare and exercise to surgery and drug use. Wikipedia notes that so-called hardmaxxing includes substances intended to increase stature, and that the term originated on incel message boards in the 2010s before spreading to TikTok in the early 2020s.[1]

Short men are called 'manlets' in forum slang, and forum users often measure themselves against thresholds such as 5 ft 10 in or 6 ft. 'Short king' is a more recent, largely mainstream phrase for shorter men with confidence and appeal, used humorously and affirmingly on social media. Its adherents generally reject the premise that height should define a man's value.

sections.h: Research on height and social outcomes
paras: Heightism is defined as prejudice or discrimination based on height.[3] Researchers have studied it in work, dating, health and well-being, and the findings differ in strength.

Earnings and work: A 2004 study by Judge and Cable reported that height was linked to workplace success for men, with income rising with height after controlling for other factors. A 2004 economic analysis by Persico, Postlewaite and Silverman estimated a wage premium of about 1.8 percent per extra inch and linked height at age 16 to adult wages.[3] Wikipedia also reports that fewer than 3 percent of CEOs in a mid-1990s survey were under 1.70 m.[3] Elsewhere in the human height literature, sex and socioeconomic status are suggested as explanations for part of the occupational gap.[8]

Dating and marriage: Earlier studies found taller men were more likely to marry and have children, and research summarised by Dan Ariely reported that American women preferred taller men and that shorter men would need higher incomes to appear equally attractive.[3] A 2015 study by Sohn reported that people trade off height against other traits such as wages or education.[3] Wikipedia's article on sexual selection in humans lists height among the traits women weigh, citing Pawlowski and colleagues' 2000 Nature paper on tall men's reproductive success.[9] A 2009 study of Hadza foragers by Sear and Marlowe found height did not influence mate choice, which commentators take to suggest that the preference is shaped by culture.[3]

Well-being: A 2005 Swedish study by Magnusson and colleagues associated each additional 5 cm of height with an approximately 9 percent lower suicide risk in men, while later studies by Coste (2012) and Griffiths (2017) found height had only a small effect on quality of life or well-being.[3][10] A 2023 study in Psychophysiology reported that young men dissatisfied with their height showed attention biases toward height-related words.[3]

Stated preferences and real pairings can differ, and two analyses address this directly. A 2013 PLoS One study by Stulp and colleagues used 12,502 heterosexual parent couples from the UK Millennium Cohort Study and compared their height differences with 10,000 simulations of random pairing.[4] Partners' heights correlated at r =.18, men were taller than their partners in 92.5 percent of couples against 89.8 percent expected by chance, and couples in which the man was 25 cm or more taller were slightly less common than chance. The authors concluded that previously documented preferences were reflected in actual couples but that the effects were modest, and they pointed to mutual choice, competition and trade-offs with other traits.[4]

A 2017 meta-analysis in the American Journal of Human Biology by Stulp, Simons, Grasman and Pollet pooled 154 correlations from 43 countries and found a moderate positive correlation between partners' heights, r =.23, in western and non-western samples alike.[5] The authors concluded that height is probably not a major factor in mate choice, while noting large unexplained variation between studies.[5] Proponents of the heightpill read the same literature as showing that preferences exist and are measurable; researchers describe the realised effects as modest.[4][5]

A central heightpill premise is that adult height is largely set. Twin studies cited in the Human height article estimate that height is roughly 60 to 80 percent heritable, with hundreds of genetic variants identified in genome-wide studies, and environmental factors such as nutrition also matter; industrialised countries gained up to 10 cm after the mid-19th century before gains levelled off.[8] The same article reports an association between greater height and a smaller life expectancy, an estimated loss of about half a year per added centimetre in several studies, and a higher cancer risk.[8] Forum members also discuss growth into the late teens, and a 13-year-old poster in one thread describes worry that his adult height is already determined.[11]

Looksmax.org has many threads titled around the heightpill, including a long-running megathread and threads such as 'heightpill is real and heres why', 'heightpill deniers are just bluepillers with extra steps', and 'heightpill nutritionpill'.[12][10] In one thread, a member argues that people who deny it do not appreciate the presence that men over 6 feet bring into a room, and describes feeling overlooked at 5 ft 4 in as a young teenager.[11] Another poster argues that masculine traits such as height, frame, voice, and large hands and feet can outweigh facial attractiveness.[13] Other threads debate whether 5 ft 10 in is still enough, and compare the heightpill with the racepill.[6][7]

Within the forums, the heightpill is often framed as a hard limit that no amount of skincare or grooming changes, which pushes discussion toward the few height-related levers members mention: footwear with hidden lifts, posture, a wider frame through training, and limb lengthening surgery. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists growth hormone among substances used in hardmaxxing for stature.[1]
Short-king content, by contrast, is mainstream social-media humor and encouragement aimed at men of shorter stature.

Advocates of the short-king framing say that confidence, grooming, humour and personality matter more than height, and point to well-known shorter men as examples. Researchers have reported that people's stated ideal heights vary by survey, for instance a 2019 Hungarian Ipsos survey in which most respondents named a range of roughly 1.78 to 1.85 m as ideal for men.[3] The research summarised above shows that height is one of several traits people weigh against each other, and that the effects found in real couples are modest.[3][4]

From the appearance angle, the short-king framing directs attention to presentation: fit and tailoring, hair and skin, posture and a confident bearing. Heightpill forum members treat these as secondary to height, while short-king advocates treat them as the main route to looking and feeling attractive.[11][13]

Wikipedia's article on heightism traces modern Western height discrimination to 19th-century eugenic and Social Darwinist movements, beginning with Francis Galton's work on parent-child height correlation, though that claim carries a verification tag on the page.[3] Sociologist Saul Feldman presented a paper on heightism to the American Sociological Association in 1971; the word then appeared in the Second Barnhart Dictionary of New English and in a 1971 Time article.[3] Historical accounts of height discrimination in antiquity are uncommon.[3]

The online heightpill belongs to the later history of looksmaxxing, which began on incel message boards in the 2010s, including the PSL forums, before moving to TikTok and other platforms in the early 2020s.[1]

Some jobs set height requirements, such as US military pilots and flight attendants.[3] On legal protection, Wikipedia lists Michigan as the only US state prohibiting height discrimination, local rules in Santa Cruz and San Francisco, a New York City rule covering height and weight, personal-appearance protections in Washington, D.C., protections in Ontario and Victoria, and a 2022 Spanish Supreme Court ruling that police height requirements must reflect each sex's population average.[3] It also lists a 2005 Swedish labour court ruling that Volvo's height requirement for female applicants was discriminatory.[3]

Media treatments cited include the 1987 BBC comedy A Small Problem, which depicted a society discriminating against people under 5 feet, the 2008 documentary S&M Short and Male, the 2019 film Tall Girl, and Tanya Osensky's 2017 book Shortchanged, which challenges heightism.[3] Wikipedia also reports a Swedish study of 1,299,177 men and notes research suggesting heightism has little effect on quality of life overall, with effects concentrated among people at the extremes of height and those dissatisfied with their own height.[3]

People who want to look taller discuss several routes. Footwear with built-in lifts adds apparent height while worn, and posture and strength training change how tall a person stands and how broad the frame looks. These are general practices and are covered in other entries.

Cosmetic limb lengthening is the surgical route. Wikipedia traces the technique to Bernhard von Langenbeck's 1869 proposal and Alessandro Codivilla's 1905 clinical report, with Gavriil Ilizarov's external fixation work from the 1950s making it widespread.[2] The procedure involves cutting the bone and gradually separating the pieces over time, followed by a consolidation period and often a second operation to remove hardware.[2] The same article reports that China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects, and that in India it is in demand but described as unregulated, with some patients reporting infections and extra surgeries.[2] Reported complication rates in general limb-lengthening include infection around 5 percent and hardware failure of 3 to 4.5 percent.[2]

Orthopaedic authors have debated the practice. A 2020 paper by Lee, Aulisio and Liu examined the ethics of lengthening in people without skeletal deformity and discussed 'height dysphoria' as a possible condition that could justify it, concluding that more work was needed to establish it.[10] A 2025 'Clinical Faceoff' in Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research, by Sabharwal, Paley and Birch, debated the role of elective bilateral lower limb lengthening for gaining height.[10]

No studies found on the heightpill or short-king discourse themselves. Related research on height, partner choice and well-being is summarised above, including a cohort analysis of 12,502 couples and a meta-analysis of 154 partner-height correlations.[4][5]

lore.intro: Heightpill is among the most frequently invoked concepts on looksmax.org, where members debate how much height outweighs face and other traits, and the short-king movement is its mainstream counterpart.[11][13][10]

Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical limb-lengthening report.[2]
Sociologist Saul Feldman presents his heightism paper; the term enters dictionaries and Time.[3]
BBC comedy A Small Problem depicts discrimination against people under 5 feet.[3]
Pawlowski, Dunbar and Lipowicz publish 'Tall men have more reproductive success' in Nature.[9]
Economic studies report a height premium in earnings.[3]
Magnusson and colleagues report an inverse link between height and suicide in 1,299,177 Swedish men.[10]
China's Ministry of Health bans limb lengthening.[2]
Study of Hadza foragers finds no height effect on mate choice.[3]
Stulp and colleagues compare height preferences with 12,502 real couples.[4]
Osensky publishes Shortchanged; Stulp and colleagues publish a height assortative-mating meta-analysis.[3][5]
Ethics paper on stature lengthening and 'height dysphoria' is published.[10]
New York City adds height and weight discrimination protections.[3]
